To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dietary fibers and fiber-like materials bind bile acids and cholesterol from micellar mixtures, that these materials bind to a greater or lesser extent depending on the nature of the fiber and the nature of the micelle, and that the binding properties of dietary fibers and fiberlike materials may be related to their hypocholesterolemic properties.
Dietary fibers and fiber components can reduce the absorption of cholesterol, phospholipid, and bile salts from mixed micelles.

Dietary fiber and fiber components bind bile salts, cholesterol and phospholipids from mixed micelles in vitro, and this is reasonably correlated with their hypocholesterolemia and other hypocholesterolemic properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a variety of aspects of bile salt metabolism, and with the effects of bile salt sequestering agents on the metabolism of cholesterol and other lipids in the rat and man.
the effects of dietary fibers on the absorption, transport and metabolism of lipids.
the effects of dietary fibers and fiber fractions on the metabolism of cholesterol and bile acids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

dietary fibers, especially the viscous gums, have some ability to bind bile salts and phospholipids from micelles, but not to an extent which would significantly affect the rate or amount of micellar lipids absorbed.

the bile acid sequestration of the bile acid sequestering resins is the primary mechanism by which they reduce the absorption of cholesterol and other lipids, and that this effect is largely unaffected by the simultaneous presence of phospholipids or cholesterol in micelles.

the binding of bile salts, lecithin, oleic acids and cholesterol from mixed bile salt micelles by bile salt sequestering resins and dietary fibers is a function of the chemical nature of both the sequestering material and the bile salt micelle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding of bile salt, cholesterol and phospholipids by bile acid sequesters and dietary fibers is a function of the chemical structure of the binding material.

dietary fibers and bile acid sequestration resins are not equivalent in their ability to bind bile salts, phosphatidylcholines and cholesterol from micellar solutions, and the relative extent of binding is not a simple function of the fiber or resin’s viscosity, or its capacity to bind bile salts from aqueous solutions.
the sequestrating properties of bile-acid sequestering resins and dietary fibers are largely determined by the bile salt content of the micelles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dietary fibers are not as good as bile-acid-sequestrant resins in removing cholesterol from the body, but they are better at removing cholesterol from the gut.
the binding of bile acids, phospholipid or cholesterol by these resins or fibers does not appear to be a simple function of the chemical structure of these compounds.
dietary fibers can sequester cholesterol and bile salts, but they are not as efficient as cholestyramin and DEAE-Sephadex.
